What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?

Long format data refers to multiple rows for each observational unit (e.g. recurring ID numbers for test scores such as math/reading)–this is generally the preferred format for statistical analysis because it is expected by many R functions from visualization libraries (ggplot2) to statistical modeling functions (lm/ANOVA/mixed effects models).
Wide format data generally has one row for each observational unit with different measurements separated by columns (e.g. one ID number followed by a math column and a reading column).


Task 2: Note: Use Chaining where possible!


Glass data

#Importing glass data to glass variable
glass <- read.table(
  "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/glass.data",
  sep = ",",
  header = FALSE
  )
names(glass) <- c(
  "ID", "RI", "Na", "Mg", "Al", "Si", "K", "Ca", "Ba", "Fe", "Type_of_glass"
)


Start a chain on your data object that overwrites the Type_of_glass variable using mutate().


glass_filtered <- glass |>
  #Map numeric codes to descriptive character factors using all 7 defined levels
  mutate(
    Type_of_glass = factor(
      Type_of_glass,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
      labels = c(
      "building_windows_float_processed",
      "building_windows_non_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_non_float_processed",
      "containers",
      "tableware",
      "headlamps"
      )
    )
  )


Continue your chain and keep only observations where the Fe variable is less than 0.2 and the Type of Glass is either “tableware” or “headlamp”.


glass_filtered <- glass |>
  mutate(
    Type_of_glass = factor(
      Type_of_glass,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
      labels = c(
      "building_windows_float_processed",
      "building_windows_non_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_non_float_processed",
      "containers",
      "tableware",
      "headlamps"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  #Keep only low-iron observations for tableware and headlamp types
  filter(
    Fe < 0.2,
    Type_of_glass %in% c("tableware", "headlamps")
  )



Yeast data

yeast <- read.table("https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/yeast.data", 
  header = FALSE, 
  col.names = c("seq_name", "mcg", "gvh", "alm", "mit", "erl", "pox", "vac", "nuc", "class")
)


Start a chain that removes the seq_name and nuc columns.


yeast_summary <- yeast |>
  #Remove identifier columns
  select(-seq_name, -nuc)


Continue your chain to add columns corresponding to the mean and median of each numeric variable (mcg, gvh, alm, mit, erl, pox, and vac) at each class grouping (see the across() function)


yeast_summary <- yeast |>
  #Remove identifier columns
  select(-seq_name, -nuc) |>
  #Group by class to calculate statistics per category
  group_by(class) |>
  #Compute mean/median across all numeric columns
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mcg, gvh, alm, mit, erl, pox, vac),
      list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )

#yeast_summary



Wine data

#Importing Wine Data via HW3 code
white_wine_url <- "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/white-wine.xlsx"
download.file(white_wine_url, destfile = "white-wine.xlsx", mode = "wb")

white_wine <- read_excel("white-wine.xlsx", sheet = 1)

white_wine_names <- read_excel("white-wine.xlsx", sheet=2)

colnames(white_wine) <- white_wine_names[[1]]

white_wine <- white_wine |>
  mutate(type = "white")

red_wine <- read_delim(file = "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/red-wine.csv", delim = ";")

Rows: 1599 Columns: 12
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ";"
dbl (12): fixed acidity, volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlo...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

colnames(red_wine) <- white_wine_names[[1]]

red_wine <- red_wine |>
    mutate(type = "red")

wine <- bind_rows(red_wine, white_wine)


Start a chain on your new combined data object to filter the data to only look at high-quality wines (quality > 6.5) and wines that have a reasonable alcohol value (alcohol < 132)


wine_summary <- wine |>
  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  )


Continue your chain to now sort the data from highest quality to lowest.


wine_summary <- wine |>
  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(quality))


Continue your chain to select only the variables that contain acid, the alochol variable, the type variable and the quality variable.


wine_summary <- wine |>
  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(quality)) |>
  select(
    contains("acid"), alcohol, type, quality
  )


Continue your chain to add the mean and standard deviation of the alcohol variable to the data set for each setting of the quality variable.


wine_summary <- wine |>
  #Filter for high quality ratings and remove extreme outliers
  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  ) |>
  #Order quality from highest to lowest
  arrange(desc(quality)) |>
  #Select acid-related variables along with key wine attributes
  select(
    contains("acid"), alcohol, type, quality
  ) |>
  #Group by quality tier to calculate alcohol summary statistics
  group_by(quality) |>
  mutate(
    mean_alcohol = mean(alcohol, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_alcohol = sd(alcohol, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

The joined data object has two fewer observations than the original ‘HallOfFame’ table because they are not in the ‘People’ table. The observations missing from the ‘People’ table are player ID’s ‘millema99’ and ‘fowlebu99’.

Return only the playerID (manager ID), G, W, and L columns from the Managers table. Use chaining to then determine the overall win/loss records (sum of wins & sum of losses) for each of these hall of fame managers using group_by() with summarize() rather than mutate. Create a new variable that is the career win/loss percentage as column Total_W/G_managed. Sort the resulting data by the win/loss percentage variable (from largest to smallest).


manager_summary <- tbl(con, "Managers") |>
  #Select only game, win, and loss columns
  select(
    playerID, G, W, L
  ) |>
  #Group by manager to aggregate career totals in the database
  group_by(playerID) |>
  summarize(
    G_managed = sum(G, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_W = sum(W, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_L = sum(L, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(win_loss_pct = Total_W / G_managed) |>
  arrange(desc(win_loss_pct))
